Why routes, not one long journey?

People arrive with different jobs to do: an organiser needs a plan, a leader needs words and commitments, a teacher needs sources. One linear journey through twenty sections would slow most of them down, while three cards left comms teams, frontline staff and community partners without a way in. Six short routes of three steps each cover every user group in the user needs table, keep each route under an hour, and leave the grouped menus for people who want to browse. This is a design judgement that still needs testing with users; tree testing of the routes is in the research plan.

    What is in this hub

    The 2026 theme

    Honouring Our Communities

    This year's national theme, set by Black History Month UK, asks us to recognise the people whose everyday contributions shape, support and sustain Black life across the UK, and to make those contributions visible.

    Organisations taking up the theme are looking beyond the best-known historical figures to the educators, carers, volunteers, health workers, artists, entrepreneurs and community leaders whose work often goes unseen. The theme also holds that Black history is not confined to the past: it is being made now, in our workplaces and neighbourhoods.

    For the public sector this is close to home. Our services are delivered by, and for, these communities. Honouring them means seeing the colleague who runs the staff network after hours, the volunteer who connects residents to services, and the generations whose labour built the institutions we work in.

    Sources: UAL, quoting BHM UK, Nottingham Trent University, University of York.

    Themes over the years

    National themes since 2021

    Black History Month UK began in 1987. National themes are well recorded from 2021; for earlier years no national theme was found while preparing this edition, so none is shown. Wales has run its own programme, with themes such as "Movers, Shakers and Legacy Makers" in 2019. In the United States, where the month is in February, the 2026 theme marked a century of commemoration.

    The visual language

    Why the hub looks like this

    The design draws on West African visual traditions chosen for what they say about community. They are used with their meanings stated, not as decoration.

    Nkonsonkonson

    An Adinkra symbol of the Akan people of Ghana showing chain links. It stands for unity, human relations and the idea that we are linked in life and beyond. It appears on the theme poster.

    Sankofa

    An Adinkra symbol often read as "go back and fetch it": it is right to return to the past to carry forward what we need. It is the emblem of the History section and the learning poster.

    The woven strip

    The bands along each edge are an original pattern inspired by West African strip-weaving, in which narrow strips are sewn together into one cloth. It is not a copy of any named kente design. Many strips, one cloth, is the theme in miniature.

    The living weave

    The opening animation threads weft lines through points that stand for people. Each thread passes over and under the others, the way a community holds together. It stops if your device asks for reduced motion.

    Iconography

    Patterns and symbols from across Africa

    Africa has 54 countries that are members of the United Nations and somewhere between about 900 and 2,000 languages, depending on how they are counted. The motifs below come from every African Union region and from the diaspora. Each one is drawn for this hub, inspired by a tradition, and labelled with its origin, its meaning, how the hub uses it and what we avoid.

    Regions follow the African Union's five regions. Island states such as Cabo Verde, Mauritius and Seychelles are too small to show at this map scale. Map: Natural Earth, Equal Earth projection.

    Ethno-linguistic heritage

    Writing systems made in Africa

    Africa's written heritage is older and wider than many people are taught. Some scripts are thousands of years old; others were invented in the last two centuries to write African languages on their own terms.

    Wisdom

    Proverbs and sayings

    Proverbs carry history, law and humour in a few words. Each is shown in its own language with a translation and what it is usually taken to mean. Translations are summaries; check them with speakers before printing.

    Handle with care: two of the most-quoted "African proverbs", "It takes a village to raise a child" and "If you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together", have no verified African origin. Researchers asked by NPR could not trace either one. Use the attributed proverbs on this page instead. Sourced · S63Sourced · S64
    Living traditions

    Customs and traditions

    Ways of naming, gathering, celebrating and mourning from across Africa and the diaspora. Traditions vary within every community, so ask the people involved how they mark them.

    Many languages, one idea

    Words for community

    Ideas of shared work and belonging, in languages from across Africa and the diaspora. Glosses are summaries; check usage with speakers before you print them.

    Diaspora and long-standing settlement

    Black communities around the world

    African-descended communities live on every inhabited continent. Some were formed by the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, some by Indian Ocean and Arab-world trade and enslavement, and some by migration after empire. A fourth group are peoples who were never part of an African diaspora but were classed as "Black" by colonial and racial systems.

    Equal Earth projection, so continents appear at their true relative size (see the real size of Africa). Where labels would overlap, some are left off the map; every place is listed below. Routes are schematic, not shipping lanes. Dotted red lines show forced transport of enslaved people across the Atlantic; dotted blue lines show the Indian Ocean trade, which included enslavement; dashed gold lines show later voluntary migration.

    Geography

    The real size of Africa

    The world and Africa maps in this hub use the Equal Earth projection, which shows every country at its true relative area. On 4 September 2026 the UN General Assembly adopted the "Correct the Map" resolution, sponsored by African Union member states and the Bahamas, which promotes Equal Earth over the Mercator projection used in many classrooms and apps. It passed 164 to 1, with six abstentions, and is not binding.

    Same places, two projections

    Sourced · S68Areas measured from the map data

    What the maps in this hub use

    • World and Africa maps: Equal Earth, an equal-area projection published in 2018, drawn from Natural Earth country outlines.
    • UK history map: a simple projection scaled for Britain's latitude. At country scale the size distortion is small, so it is fine for locating places but not for comparing areas between continents.
    • Pins: placed from latitude and longitude, so they sit where the places really are.
    • Not shown: small island states such as Cabo Verde and Mauritius, which disappear at this scale. They are still pinned where relevant.

    Mercator still has a use: it keeps directions true, which is why it is used for sea and air navigation. The resolution does not challenge that use.

      Trade and the diaspora

        Sourced · S72Sourced · S73
        Handle with care

        Who counts as Black is a historical question

        Self-identification comes first

        Use the names communities use for themselves. Some Aboriginal Australians use "Blak" as a self-chosen identity. Andamanese peoples are the Great Andamanese, Onge and Jarawa, not "Negritos", a colonial label. Siddi and Habshi communities in India are Indian citizens with African heritage.

        Why include peoples "deemed Black"?

        Colonial law and science sorted people into races using skin colour. The label "Black" was applied to peoples across the Pacific, South Asia and Australia with very different histories from the African diaspora. Showing them makes that sorting visible. It does not claim a shared ancestry or identity.

        Mixed and adjacent heritage

        Many people are of mixed African and other heritage, or come from communities with African roots that are rarely recognised, such as Afro-Indian, Afro-Arab, Afro-Turkish and Afro-Latin communities. Public services should let people describe themselves rather than fit a fixed list.

        Maroon communities

        Maroons were people who escaped slavery and built free settlements: in Jamaica, Suriname, Colombia, Mauritius and beyond. Several are now protected heritage sites. Use the "Maroon heritage" tag to find them.

        Futures thinking

        Africa and its global presence, 2030 to 2100

        What might Africa, and African and Black communities around the world, look like by the end of this century? This section uses tools from the Government Office for Science Futures Toolkit: horizon scanning, driver mapping, scenarios, Three Horizons, visioning and backcasting. Scenarios are plausible futures to test plans against, not predictions.

        Most certain

        Demography

        Africa's population is projected to grow from about 1.55 billion in 2025 to 2.47 billion by 2050. Most people who will be adults in 2050 are already born.

        Uncertain

        How that growth plays out

        Jobs, climate, governance, trade and technology will decide whether a young, growing continent becomes the world's engine or faces deep strain. These are the scenario axes below.

        Limits

        Treat long-range numbers with care

        The UN's own range for Africa in 2100 runs from 2.7 to 5.2 billion people. Anything beyond 2050 is a structured judgement, not a forecast.

        From today's patterns to tomorrow's

        Horizon 1 is how things mostly work now and will fade. Horizon 3 is an emerging future already visible in pockets. Horizon 2 is the transition: the innovations that could carry us from one to the other.

          Policy stress-testing

          Questions for your organisation

          Test your race equality, workforce and service plans against each scenario.

          Current debates

          Reparations, the curriculum and the risk of erasure

          These are live and contested questions. Each tab sets out what has happened, with sources, and the main arguments made on each side. The hub takes no position.

          For civil servants and public sector staff: you can host and facilitate discussion of these subjects, but keep to your impartiality duties. Represent the current government position accurately, present more than one view, and do not campaign for or against a policy in your official role.
          For organisers

          Organiser toolkit

          For network chairs, EDI leads, comms teams and anyone running an activity. Your checklist progress is kept in this browser only.

          Planning checklist

          Who to bring in

          • Your race or ethnic minority staff network, as partners from the start, with time allowed for the work.
          • Your senior race champion or sponsor.
          • Internal comms and the intranet team.
          • Estates or facilities for rooms, displays and access.
          • Data protection lead for stories, photos and any ethnicity information.
          • Procurement or finance before paying speakers or buying from suppliers.
          • Local Black-led community organisations, archives, museums and libraries.
          • Cross-government: the Civil Service Race Forum and your department's networks.

          Do

            Avoid

              Accessibility

              • Caption all video and live online sessions; publish transcripts.
              • Offer British Sign Language interpretation for large events where you can.
              • Give every image and poster alternative text. The posters in this hub include it.
              • Choose step-free venues, share access information in the invitation, and offer a quiet space.
              • Ask about dietary needs when food is served, and label it.
              • Hold events at varied times so part-time, shift and regional staff can join.

              Words

              • Write "Black" with a capital B when referring to people.
              • Be specific: name the group you mean, such as Black Caribbean or Black African, rather than an umbrella term.
              • Government writing guidance advises against the acronyms ‘BAME’ and ‘BME’. See Writing about ethnicity.
              • Read Words matter on race and ethnicity, why Black and African are not the same, and terms to avoid.
              • Use the words people use for themselves, and ask when unsure.
              • See the thesaurus for preferred and non-preferred terms.

              This is general good practice, not legal advice. Check your organisation's policies, the Civil Service Code (or your sector's equivalent) and your data protection team.

              Remembrance
              A quiet space to remember
              
      
              Honouring our communities means celebrating, and it also means remembering: the ancestors, the people taken, the lives cut short, and the people who fought so others could live freely. This page is deliberately still.
              
    
              
      
              
        
        
              Your candle stays lit in this browser only.
              
      
              
        
              A minute's reflection
              
        
              Take a minute, alone or as a group, before an event begins. Some communities open gatherings by naming ancestors or pouring a libation; ask your partners before including a ritual that belongs to them.

              In memory
              Whom we remember
              Dates are listed so they can be marked through the year, not only in October.
              
    
              
  
              
  
              
    
              Getting the tone right
              Joy and remembrance, side by side
              
    
              
      
              Celebrate loudly
              Food, music, stories, achievements, jokes and the jollof debate. Black history is full of joy, invention and community, and it deserves a party.
              
      
              Remember gently
              Give slavery, colonial violence, racist killings and the Windrush scandal their own quiet moment. Don't put them next to games or giveaways, and warn people before showing distressing material.
              
      
              Let people opt in
              Some colleagues carry this history personally. Make attendance optional, offer a quiet room and signpost support, such as your employee assistance programme.
              
      
              Follow the lead of those affected
              Ask your staff network and community partners how they want ancestors and loss to be marked. Different communities do this differently.
              
    
              
  
              

              



              
  
              
    
              Food and heritage
              Pull up a chair
              
      
              Nothing says "community" like a shared pot. Food travelled with African people everywhere they went, by choice and by force, and kept memory, language and family alive. Here are dishes from across Africa and the diaspora, the ingredients behind them, and home-style recipes to cook for your team. Every family does it differently, and every family is sure theirs is right.

              Brand and media hub
              The hub's identity
              An original identity for public sector use in 2026. It is not the Black History Month UK logo; credit the national theme to Black History Month UK wherever you use it.
              
    
              
      
              The mark: three linked rings
              Gold, red and green rings, linked like the Nkonsonkonson chain: people joined in community. Keep clear space of one ring's width around it, and never stretch, rotate or recolour it.
              
      
              Tone of voice
              • Warm and joyful for celebration: food, music, achievement, invitations.
              • Quiet and respectful for remembrance: slavery, racist violence, loss.
              • Plain and specific always: short sentences, real names, dates and sources.
              • Never mix jokes into remembrance, use stereotypes, or speak for a community.

              Palette
              Contrast ratios are calculated live. Use gold ink and green ink, not bright gold or green, for text on light backgrounds.

Avatars use the ten-tone Monk Skin Tone Scale and a range of hair, head coverings and access needs. Sourced · S131
              
    
              
    
              Make an avatar
              
      
              Skin tone (Monk scale)
              
      
      
      
              
      
              Faces are deliberately simple to avoid caricature. Do not link skin tone, hair or dress to a persona's role, skills or problems.
              
  
              
  
              
    
              Inclusive iconography
              Iconography bank
              People icons in any of the ten Monk skin tones, a mixed group, or no skin tone at all, plus culture and signposting icons used across the hub. Copy any icon as SVG.
              
    
              
    
              
    
              Use people icons well
              • Show a range of tones across a page, not one "default".
              • Use "no skin tone" when a person's identity is not the point.
              • Never use skin tone alone to carry meaning; label it in words.
              • Write alt text about the role or action ("volunteer", "speaker"), not appearance, unless appearance matters.
              
    
              What we avoid
              • Exaggerated features, "tribal" clichés or costume.
              • Pairing darker tones with poverty, crime or need.
              • Sacred or ceremonial symbols as decoration.
              • Yellow "neutral" figures that quietly default to white.

              Using the kit
              Do and don't
              
    
              
      
              Do
              • Add your organisation's name in the poster settings.
              • Keep the alternative text when you reuse an image online.
              • Use real photos of your own colleagues only with their consent.
              • Credit the national theme to Black History Month UK.
              
      
              Don't
              • Use stock images of anonymous Black people as decoration.
              • Add motifs whose meaning you don't know.
              • Put celebration graphics on remembrance content.
              • Use the kit to promote a product, party or campaign.
              
    
              
  
              

              




              
  
              
    
              Setting the record straight
              Common myths, and what the evidence shows
              
      
              Preconceived ideas travel faster than footnotes. Each card leads with the fact, gives the myth it corrects, cites a source we have read, and says what the evidence does not show. Turn a card over to see the myth first if you are using it in a quiz.
              
    
              
      
      
      
              
    
              
  
              
  
              
    
              Stereotypes
              Common stereotypes, and what the evidence shows
              A stereotype is a generalisation about a whole group. Even when it seems harmless, it shapes how people are judged at work, at school and in services. We name each one briefly, then set out sourced evidence and its limits.
              
    
              
  
              
  
              
    
              In conversation
              How to correct a myth without spreading it
              Correcting a myth can repeat it. These habits keep the fact in people's memory, not the myth.
              
    
                
  
                
  
                
    
                Transparency
                What we checked, and what we dropped
                
    
                
      
                Checked for this edition
                Every fact on this page was checked against the cited page on 21 October 2026. Where a figure is commonly repeated but we could not confirm it, we left it out: for example the often-quoted size of the 1835 loan, the exact launch year of the Halo Code, and a single "true" count of African languages.
                
      
                The strongest objections
                "Roman soldiers are not a community." Agreed: the card says an African unit, not continuous settlement. "Oldest university depends on definitions." Agreed: we quote Guinness's wording, "higher-learning institution". "One study does not prove a trend." Agreed: the hiring card says so.

                          For managers and recruiters
                          Positive action and the law
                          The Equality Act 2010 lets employers take proportionate steps to help under-represented groups. It does not allow positive discrimination.
                          
    
                          
      
                          Section 158: general positive action
                          Lawful where you reasonably think people who share a protected characteristic are disadvantaged, have different needs or are under-represented, and the step is proportionate. Examples: targeted outreach, application workshops, mentoring and development programmes.
                          Sourced · S93
                          
      
                          Section 159: recruitment and promotion
                          You may treat someone more favourably only if they are as qualified as the other candidate, the group is under-represented or disadvantaged, and you do not have a policy of always doing so. Take HR and legal advice first.
                          Sourced · S94
                          
    
                          
  
                          

                          



                          
  
                          
    
                          Everyone belongs here
                          Mixed heritage and belonging
                          
      
                          Many people have more than one heritage. Someone of mixed heritage may identify fully, partly or not at all with Black history, and that can change over a lifetime. This hub is for all of them: no one has to prove how Black they are to take part, and no one should be told which part of their family history counts.
                          
    
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Sharing culture well
                          Cultural appreciation and cultural appropriation
                          
      
                          Celebrating, learning about and taking part in other people's heritage is welcome when it is done with consent, respect and credit, and not for profit. Cultural appropriation usually means taking elements of a culture without understanding, credit or permission, especially where there is an imbalance of power or someone profits.

                                A proposal for comment
                                Help run the hub all year round
                                Black history is not only for October. This proposal sets out how a small group of volunteers could run, maintain and grow the hub through the year, alongside existing networks. Comment on it, suggest changes, or say you would like to help.

                                Two words that are often confused
                                Race and ethnicity: what each means and which to use
                                People often say “race” when they mean ethnicity. The two are not the same, and UK law, official statistics and science each use them in a particular way. This page explains the difference and the rule this hub follows. Every point links to its source.
                                
    
                                
  
                                
  
                                
    
                                Not interchangeable
                                Why “Black” and “African” are not the same thing
                                Not every Black person is African, and not every African is Black. Using one word for the other erases Caribbean, Black British and other Black identities, and the Arab, Amazigh and other peoples of Africa.
                                
    
                                
  
                                
  
                                
    
                                Terms and framings
                                Terms to avoid, and terms to use with care
                                Some terms are widely regarded as offensive or inaccurate. Others are debated: people and organisations disagree, and this page sets out both views rather than pretending there is one right answer. Quotations and the names of organisations are kept as written.

                                    Arguing against ourselves
                                    Myths, disagreements and the limits of this evidence
                                    Several primary papers are behind paywalls; where so, figures come from abstracts, author manuscripts, press releases or news reports, and the source says which. Most large cohorts are in the US and use US racial categories, which do not map onto UK ethnic groups. Commercial studies (23andMe) use customers' data, which may not represent everyone. Some points (54gene, the Lacks settlement) rest on news reports only.
                                    
    
                                    
  
                                    

                                    



                                    
  
                                    Identity, not biology
                                    What it means to be Black: around the world, and the African context in the UK
                                    What 'Black' means as an identity
                                    There is no single answer to what it means to be Black. It is an identity people define for themselves, shaped by history, place, politics and law, not by biology. This page sets out how the meaning changes around the world, who the Black and African communities of the UK are, and what research reports about their lives. Every point links to its source.

                                        Five words, five different things
                                        The DEEIA lens: diversity, equity, equality, inclusion and accessibility
                                        What the five terms mean
                                        Diversity, equity, equality, inclusion and accessibility (DEEIA) are five different things, often run together. This page says what each means, what UK law requires, what government policy has been since 2022, what is measured, and where people disagree, with the strongest case on each side. It then reads every new page of the hub through all five, so you can see which dimensions each covers. Every point links to its source.
                                        Show points about:
                                        
  
                                        At a glance
                                        The five dimensions at a glance
                                        Short working definitions used on this page. The sourced detail, including where the terms are disputed, is in the next section.
                                        Diversity
                                        The range of people in a workforce or community, and valuing those differences (Acas). Describes who is present, not how they are treated.
                                        Equality
                                        Equal opportunity and fair treatment, and not treating people unfairly because of a protected characteristic. In UK law this is the frame of the Equality Act 2010 and the public sector equality duty.
                                        Equity
                                        Giving people what they need so that they have fair chances, because people do not all start from the same place. Some definitions extend this to equal outcomes, which is where the term is most disputed. "Equity" is not itself a statutory term in the UK equality duties cited here.
                                        Inclusion (and belonging)
                                        Everyone feels valued, safe to contribute and able to thrive. University and professional-body definitions frame inclusion as a sense of belonging.
                                        Accessibility
                                        Making services, content and workplaces usable by disabled people. For public sector websites and apps it is a legal requirement: WCAG 2.2 AA plus an accessibility statement. In employment it links to the Equality Act duty to make reasonable adjustments.

                                              Collecting ethnicity data
                                              Collecting ethnicity data: how, when, what stops people, and declaration rates
                                              How to capture ethnicity data
                                              How UK guidance says ethnicity should be asked, at which stage of a process, what stops people and organisations from disclosing it, and how complete the data is across the Civil Service, the NHS, law, research funding, honours, the arts, health records and policing. It applies to staff, applicants, award nominees and service users alike.

                                              Made in a personal capacity
                                              Who made this hub
                                              
    
                                              
      
                                              This hub was made in a personal capacity as a contribution to Black History Month 2026. It is not an official publication, and the views in it are not those of any employer or government department.
                                              
      
                                              Its maker's family roots are in south-west Africa, in a clan that follows a matrilineal tradition: belonging, names and inheritance pass through the mother's line. The dedication below follows that tradition.
                                              
      
                                              The hub began in October 2026 as a Black History Month contribution for colleagues across the UK public sector. It was built in its maker's own time, with AI assistance, and every figure was checked against published sources. It has since grown into a year-round hub for everyone whose roots lie in Africa and its diaspora, and it is now published openly on GitHub so that others can use it, correct it and build on it.
                                              
      
                                              It publishes no personal contact details: to give feedback or report an error, use the issue forms on GitHub (see Help run the hub) or, inside Claude, leave a comment on this page.

                                              Purpose

The last part applies to Black History Month and similar initiatives in general.
                                              
    
                                              
  
                                              
  
                                              
    
                                              Rationale
                                              Diversity, equity, equality, inclusion and accessibility
                                              
      
                                              Black history is plural. It spans a continent of 54 countries and around 2,000 languages, a diaspora on every inhabited continent, and people who are also disabled, LGBTQ+, older or young, carers, migrants, people of every faith and none, and of every class. A month that sees only one story misses most of the people it is meant to honour.
                                              
    
                                              
  
                                              
  
                                              
    
                                              Under-served and at risk
                                              People and households in vulnerable circumstances
                                              
      
                                              Disadvantage clusters. People facing racism are more likely, on average, to face other barriers too. Public services meet them at their most difficult moments, so how a service is designed matters most for them.

                                                Generative, declarative and agentic AI
                                                The hub's AI assistant
                                                Select Ask in the top bar. The assistant answers only from this hub's content, drafts text in the hub's tone, corrects myths with sources, writes objectives, and can act on the page for you: opening sections, filtering schemes and networks, filling the poster form and switching map views. Every action is logged and the poster change can be undone. It runs on your own Claude account, asks your permission first, and falls back to plain search where AI is not available.

                                                  Housekeeping
                                                  Method, limits and version
                                                  
    
                                                  
      
                                                  Method
                                                  The theme was confirmed from several organisations' published Black History Month 2026 pages. Historical items were checked against archives, museums, councils and reference pages where retrieved; the rest are labelled as reference history. All content sits in one data model that drives the pages, posters, graph and export, so a change in one place reaches all of them.
                                                  
      
                                                  Limits
                                                  The official Black History Month UK site itself was not read directly; the theme wording reaches this hub through organisations quoting it. Coverage outside England is still thin, and most sources are in English. Descriptions of cultural motifs and words are summaries that should be checked with community partners. Debates move quickly: facts are dated and reviewed on 21 October 2026. No people's stories are invented.

                                                    Disclaimer
                                                    This is an unofficial resource for public sector colleagues. It is not published or endorsed by Black History Month UK or HM Government. The annual theme is set by Black History Month UK. General guidance only, not legal or HR advice.
                                                    
      
                                                    Disclosure
                                                    Drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) and assembled in a personal capacity. Items marked "reference history" have not been checked against a source in this edition. Review before use in your organisation.
                                                    
      
                                                    Transparency
                                                    No tracking or cookies. Checklist ticks, accessibility settings, theme choice and drawer state are stored only in your own browser. Links open external sites in a new tab. All motifs are drawn for this hub, inspired by named traditions, and shown with their meanings. The Debates section presents arguments without taking a position.
